blocks.text: The instrumental answers *kim? czym?*, “(with) whom? (with) what?” Its name comes from its oldest use, the instrument or means (*jechać tramwajem*, “to go by tram”), but in everyday Polish it does much more: it follows *z* meaning “with”, it names what someone is after *być*, it’s required by verbs such as *zajmować się*, and it marks location after *nad*, *pod*, *przed*, *za* and *między*.
It is also the most regular case: one ending for each gender in the singular, and one for almost everything in the plural.
Endings
Unlike the locative, the instrumental doesn’t change the stem consonant: *Kraków → Krakowem*, *stół → stołem*. The only spelling point is *-iem* after *k* and *g*.
Use 1: z, “with”
*Z* + instrumental means “together with” or “having”:

items.en: I’m going to a concert with friends.

items.pl: Czy mógłbym rozmawiać z panią profesor?
items.en: Could I speak to the professor?

items.pl: Codziennie chodzę po mieście z mapą w telefonie.
items.en: I walk around the city with a map on my phone.

blocks.text: Two things to notice. *Z* + genitive means something different, “from”: *z Gdańska*. And “I … with X” is often expressed as “we … with X”: *pójdziemy z kolegami* means “I’ll go with my friends”, and *my z Anią* means “Ania and I.”
Use 2: means of transport and instruments
The thing you travel by or work with takes a bare instrumental, with no preposition: *jechać tramwajem, autobusem, pociągiem*; *pisać długopisem*; *jeść widelcem*.
A related use marks the route: *iść ulicą Grodzką*, “to walk along Grodzka Street”; *jechać lasem*, “to drive through the forest.”
Use 3: what someone is
After *być*, a noun that says what someone or something is goes in the instrumental. This is one of the most frequent uses in conversation:

head: Polish
English
rows: She wants to become a translator.

blocks.text: Three contrasts keep this straight. An adjective after *być* stays nominative: *jestem zmęczony*. A noun after *to* stays nominative: *To jest lekarz*, “That’s a doctor.” And *zostać*, “to become”, takes the instrumental like *być*.
Use 4: verbs that take the instrumental

head: verb
example
rows: *zajmować się*, to work on, deal with
*cieszyć się*, to enjoy, be glad of

blocks.text: Most of these are reflexive verbs with *się*. The question word follows the same case: *czym?*, *kim?*
Use 5: location with nad, pod, przed, za, między
These prepositions take the instrumental for location and the accusative for direction:
*Przed* also means “before” in time, with the instrumental: *przed obiadem*, “before lunch”; *przed świętami*, “before Christmas.”
Use 6: time of day and season

Several time words are simply instrumentals of nouns: *wieczorem*, “in the evening”; *latem*, *zimą*, *wiosną*, *jesienią*, “in summer, winter, spring, autumn”; *nocą*, “by night” (a little literary; everyday speech prefers *w nocy*).
